Published 1 October 2026 · By Steve English · Major factual claims linked to sources

ASHFIELD · LOCAL POLITICS · REFORM UK

REFORM EYES SWEEP OF ASHFIELD AS INDEPENDENTS UNRAVEL

Nine of ten county seats already belong to Reform. Now the party is targeting the district council as its main local rival faces defections, departures and leadership turmoil — with at least one member defecting to Reform UK this week.

  • Reform UK won nine of Ashfield's ten county divisions in May 2025, taking 50.0% of the vote across the district.
  • The Ashfield Independents fell from ten county divisions to one.
  • Former council leader Jason Zadrozny was convicted on 21 September 2026 of nine fraud offences and four offences of fraudulent income tax evasion.
  • Warren Nuttall announced his defection to Reform UK on 29 September and said other councillors wanted to leave.

PURPOSE / MISSION: To put one councillor's defection into the wider Ashfield picture: a dramatic county-election reversal, leadership crisis, departures and stand-downs — while Reform prepares to contest control of Ashfield District Council in 2027.

Ashfield's political landscape is undergoing a remarkable transformation.

A local political group which once dominated the area has lost nine of its ten county council seats, seen its long-standing leader convicted of fraud and tax offences, lost councillors from its ranks and watched senior figures announce that they will not stand again.

Now another Ashfield Independent councillor has announced his defection to Reform UK — and says others are considering leaving.

The significance goes far beyond the movement of a single councillor. Having already swept nine of Ashfield's ten divisions at the 2025 Nottinghamshire County Council elections, Reform is now preparing to challenge for control of Ashfield District Council itself.

And the political group standing in its way is facing serious questions about its own future.

A POLITICAL EMPIRE ALREADY SHAKEN

For years, the Ashfield Independents were an unusually powerful force in local politics.

They have controlled Ashfield District Council since 2018 and, going into the May 2025 Nottinghamshire County Council elections, Ashfield Independent district councillors represented all ten county divisions covering the district. The Local Government Association later recorded the scale of what happened next: only one Ashfield Independent retained a county seat, while Reform gained the other nine.

10Independent-held divisions before May 2025
9Won by Reform UK in 2025
1Retained by Ashfield Independents

Official Nottinghamshire results show Reform took 50.0% of the vote across Ashfield, winning nine seats to the Independents' one.

The reversal reached the top of the local group. In the Ashfields division, then council leader Jason Zadrozny lost to Reform UK's Alan Bite by 1,687 votes to 1,015.

But the electoral defeat would not be the end of the Independents' problems.

ZADROZNY CONVICTED

The crisis intensified dramatically in September.

On 21 September, former Ashfield District Council leader Jason Zadrozny was convicted at Northampton Crown Court of nine counts of fraud and four counts of fraudulent income tax evasion. Jurors acquitted him on three further fraud counts.

The court heard that the fraud included money obtained through the Ashfield Heritage Society, while the tax charges related to rental income from four properties. Zadrozny denied wrongdoing during the trial.

The following day he announced that he would resign as leader of Ashfield District Council and leave the Ashfield Independents group with immediate effect. He remained a councillor for Larwood while awaiting sentencing.

Councillor Samantha Deakin was subsequently selected as the new leader of the council.

Within days, another councillor was heading for the exit.

NUTTALL DEFECTS TO REFORM

Councillor Warren Nuttall, who represents Greenwood and Summit, announced that he had left the Ashfield Independents to join Reform UK. Open Council Data also recorded the change on 29 September.

“Jason has collapsed the Ashfield Independents.”

Warren Nuttall, quoted by the Local Democracy Reporting Service

More significantly, Nuttall suggested his departure might not be the last.

“There are a lot more who want to leave; they just don't know which way to go.”

Warren Nuttall

That matters because Nuttall is not the only councillor publicly questioning the future of the organisation.

“THE ASHFIELD INDEPENDENTS ARE DONE”

Earlier in 2026, Councillor Kier Barsby had already left the Ashfield Independents and become an unaligned councillor. Ashfield District Council formally recorded the change in February after receiving his political-group notification on 20 January.

Following the latest turmoil, Barsby's assessment was unequivocal:

“The Ashfield Independents are done.”

Kier Barsby

Others have stopped short of going that far, but several senior figures have already decided that they will not contest the next district elections.

New council leader Samantha Deakin has said she will not stand again. Councillor Matt Relf, the council's lead member for growth, regeneration and local planning, has also confirmed that he will not seek another term.

Relf nevertheless told the LDRS that there were members who wanted the organisation to continue and that it needed “fresh energy”.

“EVERYONE IS AT A POINT OF REFLECTION”

Ashfield Independent Councillor Lee Waters has publicly called for Zadrozny to resign his council seat following his convictions.

Asked about his own future with the Ashfield Independents, Waters did not rule out leaving.

“At the moment, feelings are quite raw. Everyone is at a point of reflection.”

Lee Waters

Taken individually, any one of these developments might represent the normal movement and retirement which occurs within local politics. Taken together, they paint a very different picture.

The Ashfield Independents have gone from holding all ten of Ashfield's county divisions to holding one. Their former leader has been convicted and has left the group. Councillors have departed. Senior members have announced that they will not stand again. One former member says the organisation is finished. Another has announced his defection to Reform and says others want to leave.

REFORM'S NEXT TARGET: THE DISTRICT COUNCIL

That leaves one much bigger political question hanging over Ashfield: what happens at the next district council election?

All 35 district council seats are due to be contested in May 2027. Ashfield Reform UK says it has begun its candidate-selection process and explicitly states that it wants to take control of Ashfield District Council.

That is Reform's stated objective, not an election result in waiting. Voters will decide who controls the authority in 2027.

But the political transformation which has already taken place is substantial. In little more than a year, Reform has taken nine of Ashfield's ten county divisions, while the Ashfield Independents have gone from near-total dominance at county level to a single seat.

Now Reform is gaining support at district level while the Independents face perhaps the most serious internal crisis in their history.

REFORM HAS ALREADY SWEPT THE COUNTY SEATS.
NOW IT HAS ASHFIELD DISTRICT COUNCIL IN ITS SIGHTS.
